books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, A. Political Parties and the Rise of the First Two-Party System

stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1801, public domain (Avalon Project text). Abridged with ellipses.
stimulus.text:
“Every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We have called by different names brethren of the same principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists. … Equal and exact justice to all men, of whatever state or persuasion, religious or political; peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none; the support of the State governments in all their rights, as the most competent administrations for our domestic concerns, and the surest bulwarks against anti-republican tendencies; the preservation of the General Government in its whole constitutional vigor, as the sheet anchor of our peace at home and safety abroad.”
— Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1801 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from Jefferson's First Inaugural Address (1801)
stem: Jefferson's claim that every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle most directly responded to which development?

options.text: The Hartford Convention, where New England Federalists discussed leaving the Union
options.misconception: The Hartford Convention met in 1814, thirteen years after this speech, so it cannot be what Jefferson was answering.

options.text: The bitter campaign of 1800, in which Federalists warned Jefferson would bring terror
The Missouri Compromise, which divided the Louisiana Territory over slavery
options.misconception: The Missouri Compromise came in 1820, long after Jefferson left office, and it was about slavery, not party feeling.

options.text: The Nullification Crisis, in which South Carolina tried to void a federal tariff
options.misconception: The Nullification Crisis came in 1832, during Jackson's presidency, decades after this address.

rationales.A: The Hartford Convention met in 1814, thirteen years after this speech, so it cannot be what Jefferson was answering.
rationales.B: The 1800 campaign was vicious on both sides. Federalists warned that Jefferson would bring French-style terror, and Democratic-Republicans called Adams a would-be king. Jefferson's line answers that fear directly: disagreement does not make the other side an enemy of the republic.
rationales.C: The Missouri Compromise came in 1820, long after Jefferson left office, and it was about slavery, not party feeling.
rationales.D: The Nullification Crisis came in 1832, during Jackson's presidency, decades after this address.
rationales.general:
1. Date the speech. Jefferson speaks in March 1801, just after the election of 1800.
2. Recall the campaign. Both parties smeared the other candidate as a danger to liberty itself.
3. Read the line against that fear. Jefferson says a difference of opinion is not a difference of principle.
4. Put it together. He is telling a frightened country that partisan disagreement is not treason.
Remember: to understand a speech, start with the fight it was written to end.
